analysis: Examined the four files in this batch. Darkbloom.swift head line 32 registers a new `Addon` subcommand. Its implementation (Addon.Status/Hold/Release, Addon.liveIdentity, Addon.describe, AddonHoldView/AddonHoldSnapshot, DaemonState.addonHold) is not in this batch. StatusCommand+AddonHold.swift (head 1-13) and StatusCommand.swift head 118 add a display-only line built from the daemon state file's addonHold snapshot. It reads the local owner state file, which carries no secrets, so it adds no new exposure. AddonCommandTests.swift shows the intended contract: lease 30-600s, default 600; `release --force`; liveIdentity needs a fresh state file, a current process identity and a non-nil addonHold. Tests also show holds persist in daemon-state.json under addon_hold, and a hold is kept past lease expiry while a machine lock is held (add-on VMs may be running). These items are new attack surface not covered by the threat model and need integration review. (1) How does the hold CLI reach the daemon: IPC, socket or file? Can any local process acquire or release holds? This compares to TB-010/T-044 lease impersonation; the impact is availability only, but the operator already controls the box. (2) Does a hold correctly stop the coordinator from routing inference, and is the hold reported to the coordinator? Do queued requests drain? This touches TB-002/T-053. (3) Add-on VMs co-resident with the provider process: what isolates them from decrypted prompts (A-001), the X25519 key (A-003), GPU memory (T-028) and the KV cache (T-041)? Are VMs granted any privilege? Does 'kept while machine lock held' allow an unbounded hold? (4) TB-003/TB-011: is an add-on machine lock compatible with App Attest/attestation claims, and is the threat-model scope missing an add-on boundary? No concrete regression is visible in the supplied lines; the batch contains only CLI wiring and status display.
